intro: The F♯-major Nocturne places an ornamented singing line above a supporting accompaniment, then interrupts that poise with a faster central section. Luke Faulkner’s recording is a modern counterpart to the historical performances: follow the same melody, but ask how its timing and balance are shaped.
question: How does the opening melody sound different after the faster middle?

sections.label: A′ · Larghetto returns
sections.mNote: the opening song returns after the faster middle

cues.title: A decorated singing line
cues.text: Follow the main melody through its ornaments rather than treating every quick note as equally important. The accompaniment supports a slower phrase underneath the surface decoration.
cues.evidence: Opening song and ornamental writing described by Tomaszewski: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

cues.title: Dedicated to Ferdinand Hiller
cues.text: Chopin dedicated the three nocturnes of Op. 15 to Ferdinand Hiller. The dedication belongs to the history of the published collection; it does not turn the second Nocturne into a portrait of its dedicatee.
cues.evidence: NIFC work record names Ferdinand Hiller: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

cues.title: The opening contains contrast
cues.text: Even before the faster middle, the opening region has a contrasting minor-key idea. Listen for changes in the melodic direction and harmonic colour, not only for changes of speed.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the F-sharp-minor counter-theme within the opening region: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173. This cue describes the surrounding span, not its exact onset.

cues.title: A work of the early 1830s
cues.text: The Nocturne dates from 1830–33. Its compact return form already gives the singing melody a dramatic setting: the central contrast changes how a listener hears material that was initially self-contained.
cues.evidence: Composition dating and reprise form in https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

cues.title: Twice the motion
cues.text: The central section is marked doppio movimento, with an initially subdued sotto voce character. Faster motion is not the same instruction as immediate loudness; the passage has room to build after the change of pace.
cues.evidence: Estimated middle at the strongest report boundary,1:26; the following windows rise towards a1:50 crest. Score headings and dramatic trajectory: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The middle draws back
cues.text: After the central rise, the sound rapidly subsides. Listen for the reduction in momentum that allows the opening song to return without sounding like another forceful interruption.
cues.evidence: Report level falls steeply from the crest around 1:50 into the quiet 2:05–2:10 windows. This is an amplitude contour, not an estimate of written dynamics.

cues.title: The singing line returns
cues.text: The opening’s slower melodic character returns after the turbulent middle. Compare its phrasing with the beginning: the return restores the theme, but the intervening contrast changes the listener’s frame of reference.
cues.evidence: Approximate return at2:12, after the low2:10 window and before renewed F-sharp-major-coloured activity at2:15. Reprise form: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A German first edition
cues.text: Breitkopf & Härtel’s first edition of the three nocturnes appeared in early 1834. The surviving printed score lets listeners distinguish Chopin’s tempo and articulation instructions from choices made by a particular recorded performer.
cues.evidence: NIFC digital score record gives January–February1834 for the German first edition: https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

cues.title: Let the last sound decay
cues.text: At the close, attend to the space after the final gestures as well as to their attacks. The recording preserves a decay, but it does not by itself identify which piano, room or microphone produced that sound.
cues.evidence: Late report windows decline towards the204-second end. Source documentation leaves instrument, venue and recording technique unknown.

transitions.title: The song yields to a faster inner pulse
transitions.how: The ornamented Larghetto gives way to a middle marked doppio movimento and sotto voce. Faster articulation changes the sense of movement before the section develops its full dynamic force. The contrast therefore begins with tempo and texture, not with an instruction to play every note loudly.
transitions.evidence: Strong report boundary1:26; level rises thereafter towards1:50. Markings and central design: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

transitions.title: The central surge subsides into the song
transitions.how: The faster middle retreats and the Larghetto melody returns. Its ornamental surface and supporting accompaniment recover the opening balance after the concentrated central activity. A decrease in density and force helps make the familiar song audible as a return rather than a fresh episode.
transitions.evidence: Report falls steeply at2:00–2:10 and recovers around2:15; the2:12 marker is approximate. Formal reprise: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
